title: Motility-Induced Phase Separation of Run-and-Tumble Particles under Local Stochastic Resetting
abstract: We investigate the non-equilibrium stationary states of a one-dimensional active gas composed of run-and-tumble particles (RTPs) undergoing motility-induced phase separation (MIPS) and subjected to local stochastic resetting at the origin. Unlike global resetting, local resetting maintains a mass-injection flux at the origin while preserving large-scale spatial self-organization. We demonstrate that above a critical resetting rate $r_c$, the active system undergoes a transition toward a stationary two-phase state featuring a dense liquid droplet centered at the origin coexisting with a surrounding gas phase. Using kinetic evolution equations, we derive the exact steady-state density profile expressed in terms of the Lambert function. The size of the droplet has a non-monotonic dependence on the resetting rate $r$, and attains its maximum. Furthermore, we analyze the dynamical stability of the supersaturated gas phase and show that a nucleated droplet relaxes exponentially toward its steady-state size with a relaxation timescale of $1/r$. We extend our framework to model a finite resetting velocity, proving that the stationary droplet size is invariant with respect to the resetting velocity.
summary: This paper theoretically analyzes how run-and-tumble particles exhibiting Motility-Induced Phase Separation behave when subjected to local stochastic resetting. It finds that above a critical rate, the system stabilizes into a distinct liquid droplet coexisting with a gas phase. The work provides exact analytical solutions for the density profiles and characterizes the size dependence of this phase separation.
main_problem: The study investigates the non-equilibrium stationary states of an active gas undergoing Motility-Induced Phase Separation (MIPS) when subjected to local stochastic resetting.
main_result: The system undergoes a transition to a stationary two-phase state (liquid droplet in a gas background) above a critical resetting rate, and the droplet size exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the resetting rate.
method: The analysis uses kinetic evolution equations to derive the exact steady-state density profile in both the gas and liquid phases, solving the resulting differential equations.
model_or_system: The model is a one-dimensional active gas composed of Run-and-Tumble Particles (RTPs) whose motility is density-dependent, and which are subjected to local stochastic resetting at the origin.
key_observables: Stationary two-phase density profile, droplet size ($b$), relaxation timescale of the droplet, and the density profile in the surrounding gas phase.
important_parameters: Critical resetting rate ($r_c$), density of movers ($ho_m$), and the resetting rate ($r$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes parity symmetry and relies on piecewise definitions for the particle velocity based on density thresholds.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spatial configuration of the steady state (liquid droplet/gas phase), the dependence of droplet size on the resetting rate, and the exponential time evolution of the droplet mass.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by deriving the stationary state equations, analyzing the interface equilibrium conditions, solving the resulting differential equations for both phases, and finally analyzing the dynamics of droplet nucleation and the extension to finite resetting velocity.
why_interesting: While focused on classical active matter, the non-equilibrium nature, phase transitions, and the use of continuous kinetic equations for steady states are highly relevant to open quantum systems and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Spatial configuration of the steady state with a central liquid droplet of half-width b. The particle velocity v(ρ) switches from a density-dependent profile in the gas phase to a uniform minimum value inside the saturated liquid phase.
Figure 2: Exact droplet half-width b as a function of resetting rate r. The droplet emerges at rc, reaches maximum extent at r∗, and contracts asymptotically for large r.

Figure 3: Stationary spatial density profile ρ(x) (logarithmic scale) representative parameters. For r < rc there is a discontinuity at x = b. The density in the entire space is obtained by parity symmetry.

Figure 4: Time evolution of droplet mass Mliq(t) nucleating at the origin in a supersaturated gas (for implementation, v0 = 1, α = 1, ρm = 1, 000 M = 289 > 2/χ, r = 0.5), confirming exponential relaxation with rate r. Stars indicate the values obtained by direct numerical simulation of the system, as described in Appendix A.
Figure 5: Phase diagram. In the domain between the two curves, there are two steady states, one of which is a supersaturated gas. The values used in the plot are ρm = 5, α = 1, v0 = 1.
